source_text: In inferioribus itaque libri tui partibus postquam dixisti: Sic creat malos Deus, quomodo pascit et nutrit malos, addis: Quia, quod eis creando tribuit, ad naturae pertinet bonitatem et, quod eis pascendo et nutriendo dat incrementum, non utique malitiae eorum, sed eidem bonae naturae, quam creavit bonus, bonum tribuit adiumentum. In quantum enim homines sunt, bonum est naturae, cuius auctor est Deus; in quantum autem cum peccato nascuntur perituri, qui non renascuntur, ad semen pertinet maledictum ab initio illius antiquae inoboedientiae vitio [n183] . Quo tamen bene utitur factor etiam vasorum irae, ut notas faciat divitias gloriae suae in vasis misericordiae, ut non meritis suis tribuat, si ad eamdem massam quisque pertinens gratia liberetur, sed " qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur " [n184] . Ab hac fide iste discedens non vult nascentes esse sub diabolo, ne parvuli portentur ad Christum, ut eruantur a potestate tenebrarum et in regnum ipsius transferantur [n185] . Et sic Ecclesiam accusat toto orbe diffusam, in qua ubique omnes baptizandi infantuli non ob aliud exsufflantur, nisi ut ab eis mundi princeps mittatur foras [n186] . Item deorsum de libidine loquens, sine qua coniugum non potest esse commixtio, quam nos naturalem et ad Dei operam pertinentem non ut magnum aliquod bonum, sed ut sensum corporum, quae sunt a Deo facta, defendimus, quam tu inditam visceribus humanis a diabolo atque in eius verecundia dogma tuum collocans tam multis scriptis conaris asserere, de ipsa ergo libidine, sicut frequenter, ita etiam in inferiore parte libri tui loqueris: Quocirca - inquis - commixtionem quoque honestam coniugum non reprehendimus propter pudendam libidinem corporum. Illa enim posset esse nulla praecedente perpetratione peccati, de qua non erubescerent coniugati; haec autem exorta est post peccatum, quam coacti sunt velare confusi [n187] . Unde remansit posterioribus coniugatis, quamvis hoc malo bene et licite utentibus, in eiusmodi opere humanum vitare conspectum atque ita confiteri, quod pudendum est, cum debeat neminem pudere, quod bonum est. Proinde pudenda libidine, qui licite concumbit, malo bene utitur; qui autem illicite, malo male utitur [n188] .
pass_a_gloss: In the inferior parts therefore of your book after you have said: Thus God creates evils as he feeds and nourishes evils, you add: Because what he has attributed to them by creating pertains to the goodness of nature, and what he gives them increase by feeding and nourishing, he attributes a good help not indeed to their malice but to the same good nature which the good created. For insofar as they are humans, it is the good of nature whose author is God; but insofar as they are born with sin about to perish, who are not reborn, it pertains to the seed cursed from the beginning by the vice of that ancient disobedience. Which nevertheless the maker even of vessels of wrath uses well, that he may make known the riches of his glory in vessels of mercy, that he not attribute to his own deserts, if anyone pertaining to the same mass is freed by grace, but he who glories, let him glory in the Lord. Departing from this faith this one does not want those being born to be under the devil, lest little ones be carried to Christ, that they may be plucked from the power of darkness and transferred into his kingdom. And thus he accuses the Church diffused through the whole orb, in which everywhere all little infants to be baptized are blown upon for no other reason except that from them the prince of the world be sent outside. Likewise downward speaking of lust, without which there cannot be a mixing of spouses, which we defend as natural and pertaining to the work of God not as some great good but as a sense of bodies which have been made by God, which you want implanted in human viscera by the devil and, placing your dogma in the shame of it, you try to assert by so many writings, about that lust therefore, as frequently, so also in the inferior part of your book you speak: For which reason, you say, we also do not reprehend the honest mixing of spouses on account of the shameful lust of bodies. For that could have been with no preceding perpetration of sin, of which the married would not blush; but this has arisen after sin, which the confused have been forced to veil. Whence it has remained to later married persons, although using this evil well and licitly, in a work of this kind to avoid human sight and thus to confess that it is to be ashamed of, when no one ought to be ashamed of what is good. Accordingly who lies licitly by shameful lust uses an evil well; but who illicitly uses an evil badly.

lemmas.lexica: LS libido; Blaise often sexual desire; Julian treats as created sensation, not a sin-nature
LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS gratia=favor; Blaise grace; in iustitia definitions often 'favoritism'

pass_b_english: In the later parts of your book, after saying, ‘God creates evil people in the same way as he feeds and nourishes evil people,’ (John 12:31) you add:

‘For what he gives them by creating them belongs to the goodness of nature. When he gives them growth by feeding and nourishing them, he gives good assistance not to their wickedness but to that same good nature which he, being good, created. Insofar as they are human, there is the good of nature, whose author is God. But insofar as they are born with sin and will perish unless reborn, this belongs to the seed cursed from the beginning by the fault of that ancient disobedience (compare Wisdom 12:11). Yet the maker of even the vessels of wrath uses this well to make known the riches of his glory in vessels of mercy (Romans 9:22–23). Thus, if anyone belonging to the same mass is freed by grace, he should not credit his own merits, but “let the one who boasts boast in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1:31).

‘Departing from this faith, this man refuses to allow that newborns are under the devil, so that infants will not be brought to Christ to be rescued from the power of darkness and transferred into his kingdom (Colossians 1:13). In this way he accuses the Church spread throughout the world, in which everywhere all infants about to be baptized are breathed upon in exorcism for no other reason than to cast the ruler of this world out of them’ (Augustine, Marriage and Sexual Desire 2.32–33; compare John 12:31).

Again, further down, you discuss sexual desire, without which spouses cannot unite. We defend it as natural and belonging to God’s work, not as some great good, but as a sensation of bodies made by God. You maintain that the devil implanted it in human inward parts, and, founding your doctrine on the shame surrounding it, you try to establish this in so many writings. About this same desire, then, as often elsewhere, you say in a later part of your book:

‘Therefore we do not criticize the honorable union of spouses because of the body’s shameful desire. Such union could have existed without any preceding commission of sin, and spouses would not have blushed for it. But this desire arose after sin, and their confusion forced them to cover it (Genesis 3:7). Hence later spouses, although using this evil well and lawfully, still avoid human sight during such an act. They thus acknowledge something shameful, although no one ought to be ashamed of something good. Therefore anyone who has lawful intercourse through shameful desire uses an evil well, while anyone who has unlawful intercourse uses an evil badly’ (Augustine, Marriage and Sexual Desire 2.36).

choices.why: Julian distinguishes nuptiae from concupiscentia; do not flatten to 'lust' as a nature-sin substance.
Julian defends marriage as God's work against the charge that generation transmits sin.
